title: DHS proposes new $100K filing fee on H-1B visa petitions
content: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Monday published a proposal for a $103, 265 fee imposed on those filing a cap-subject petition for an H-1B visa. The new fee would apply to all H-1B petitions, regardless of if the worker is inside or outside of the US, except for those filed by universities, certain non-profits like hospitals, government positions, or visa renewals. This proposal follows the June declaration by a federal judge and a subsequent affirmation by an appeals court, that US President Trump’s previous $100,000 fee on H-1B visas violated the separation of powers doctrine and was therefore unconstitutional. As attempts to implement the original fee proved unsuccessful, at least temporarily, the Trump administration has taken a different avenue to further this piece of their agenda, using agency rule-making as opposed to presidential power . The H-1B visa program is the most common way for employers to retain temporary foreign workers in speciality positions. Visas issued under the program by US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) are capped at 65,o00 per fiscal year and the proposed fee applies to any visa petition that is not exempt from the cap. Additionally, the fee is applied on top of all other fees incurred in applying for the visa, including the previous, and potentially revivable, 100,000 fee, and it is only an application fee, not a guarantee that the visa will be approved. H-1B workers make up approximately 730,000 employees in the US and contribute an estimated $86 billion to the federal economy and $11 billion to state and local tax revenues. DHS indicated in their rule that the purpose of the fee is to recover immigration and customs related costs incurred by federal agencies in enforcing mechanisms of “the lawful immigration system.” Acquired funds will be put towards operations like immigration court proceedings, consular visa processing, enforcing labor standards, and inspection and enforcement activities
author: Abigail Austin | Vermont Law & Graduate School, US

title: Amnesty International calls for children to be included in youth digital rights regulatory processes
content: Amnesty International reported on Monday that international failure to ensure children’s online safety from Big Tech harms is connected to a lack of the youth perspective in policymaking spaces. Classifying existing solutions as performative, the organization points out that increasing surveillance, data tracking, and censorship is a major threat to their safety. Children face “r isks such as cyberbullying, grooming, online violence, and problematic social media use” while their data is “constantly collected, tracked and shared” by “a largely invisible network of government and private actors, in most cases without free and informed consent.” In a recent brief , the UN attributed these issues to technology companies that are financially incentivized to maximize revenue. These companies profit from tailoring content to users’ emotional vulnerabilities and related habits. Children are uniquely susceptible to these activities. Specifically, “algorithmic and AI systems can keep young users hooked, trapping them in harmful, never ending content loops and exposing them to increasingly extreme material, including self-harm and suicide content, pornography, extremism and violence.” Furthermore, data is tracked outside of social media in schools and universities, which collect biometric attendance data and leverage AI-enabled performance metrics. Many countries have addressed social media concerns by instituting bans for underaged children. Turkey requires platforms to establish age-verification systems and restrict age-inappropriate content access. Australia declared Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X, YouTube, Kick and Reddit to be age-restricted platforms inaccessible to children under the age of sixteen. Other countries that have enacted similar bans include Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Various countries are strongly considering such a ban, including Britain, Denmark, Greec

title: US Supreme Court lifts block on Trump mail voting executive order
content: The US Supreme Court stayed a district court injunction Monday that had blocked President Donald Trump’s executive order overhauling mail voting, ruling in a per curiam opinion that the states had not shown an injury concrete and imminent enough to make their claims justiciable before the November midterm election. In Trump v. California , No. 26A124 (a related application in Alabama v. California , No. 26A139, was denied as moot), the court found the government likely to succeed on its argument that the states’ claims are not justiciable, because it considered the order itself, in its words, “an internal directive from the President to his subordinates” that “neither requires nor forbids anything of anyone outside the Executive Branch.” Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Elena Kagan, and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson each dissented separately. Executive Order No. 14399 , issued in March, directs the US Department of Homeland Security to compile state-by-state “Citizenship List[s]” of voters, instructs the US Department of Justice to prioritize prosecuting officials who issue ballots to ineligible voters, and directs the US Postal Service to initiate a proposed rulemaking on mail ballot envelopes, including a barcode requirement. The court measured the states’ injury when they sued, before the Postal Service had proposed any rule, and found the harm too speculative to support standing. The Homeland Security Secretary may compile the lists only “to the extent feasible and consistent with applicable law,” and prosecutions are limited to conduct “consistent with applicable law.” Since then, the Postal Service has proposed the rule and finalized it , effective August 21, three days before Monday’s ruling. title: New Zealand PM introduces under-16 social media and AI companion ban
content: The New Zealand government announced on Monday that it had introduced a bill to ban social media for children under 16. The law would require social media platforms and social AI companions to verify users’ ages before providing services. The Online Safety (Minimum Age and Child Safety Risk Assessment) Bill would require an age restriction on platforms with harmful features for children. These features include recommender systems, endless feeds, feedback features and time-limited features. The bill also seeks to restrict underage users from accessing AI companion services. However, it explicitly excludes messaging apps, professional networking sites, gaming and music platforms, and other educational and health tools. Notably, age verification through self-declared dates of birth and formal identification does not satisfy the platforms’ duty under the law. It also requires platforms to verify their users’ age through other methods such as facial scans and user activity patterns. The bill would also require platforms to conduct child safety risk assessments for all users under 18 and protect them from harmful content such as bullying, violence, and sexually explicit materials. Introducing the bill, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said similar laws in Australia have demonstrated effectiveness, adding: “We have protections to keep children safe in the real world and we need them in the virtual world too.” In December 2025, Australia became the first country to ban social media for underage users. The country cited that the law has led to the deletion of over 5 million social media accounts with Prime Minister Antony Albanese vowing to strengthen the ban in June. Apart from non-compliance concerns , the government is also defending Reddit’s challenge to the ban’s constitutionality. Several countries follow or plan to follow Australia’s path on online child protection, including France , the UK , Canada , Malaysia , and Tür
